हिमाचल प्रदेश में दिवाली के बाद मौसम एक बार फिर करवट लेने वाला है। मौसम विज्ञान केंद्र के अनुसार 10 और 11 नवंबर को मध्य पर्वतीय क्षेत्रों में हल्की बारिश, जबकि ऊंचाई वाले इलाकों में बारिश के साथ बर्फबारी हो सकती है। प्रदेश में फिलहाल तापमान में उतार-चढ़ाव जारी है।

हिमाचल प्रदेश में दिवाली के बाद मौसम एक बार फिर बदलने वाला है। प्रदेश में अगले कुछ दिनों तक मौसम साफ रहने के बाद 10 और 11 नवंबर को बारिश और बर्फबारी होने के आसार हैं। मौसम विज्ञान केंद्र के पूर्वानुमान के अनुसार राज्य में 9 नवंबर तक मौसम साफ रहने की संभावना है। इसके बाद मध्य पर्वतीय क्षेत्रों में कुछ स्थानों पर हल्की बारिश हो सकती है। वहीं, उच्च पर्वतीय इलाकों में कहीं-कहीं हल्की बारिश के साथ बर्फबारी होने का पूर्वानुमान है।
शिमला में वीरवार को हल्के बादल छाए रहे। प्रदेश में इन दिनों अधिकतम और न्यूनतम दोनों तापमान में बढ़ोतरी दर्ज की जा रही है। हालांकि कुछ स्थानों पर रात के तापमान में गिरावट भी आई है। कुकुमसेरी में सबसे कम न्यूनतम तापमान माइनस 1.8 डिग्री सेल्सियस दर्ज किया गया, जबकि ऊना में अधिकतम तापमान 33.4 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहा।

इस दिन तक खिली रहेगी धूप, फिर पहाड़ों पर बदलेगा मौसम, शिमला में बर्फबारी का इंतजार अभी और बढ़ा
जानिए इस दिवाली आपके जिले में कैसा रहेगा मौसम. 9 नवंबर तक प्रदेश में दिन का तापमान सामान्य से कुछ अधिक बना रहेगा.
शिमला: हिमाचल में सर्दियों के मौसम के बीच फिलहाल धूप का दौर जारी रहने वाला है. इस दिवाली प्रदेश के विभिन्न जिलों में मौसम सामान्य रहने वला है. प्रदेशवासियों को अभी बारिश और बर्फबारी के लिए थोड़ा और इंतजार करना पड़ सकता है. मौसम विभाग के पूर्वानुमान के अनुसार, आगामी 9 नवंबर तक प्रदेशभर में मौसम साफ और शुष्क बना रहेगा. हालांकि, इसके बाद एक कमजोर पश्चिमी विक्षोभ के सक्रिय होने से पहाड़ों के मौसम में हल्का बदलाव देखने को मिल सकता है. 10 और 11 नवंबर को प्रदेश के ऊंचाई वाले क्षेत्रों में कहीं-कहीं बहुत हल्की बारिश और बर्फबारी होने की संभावना है.
हिमाचल में मौसम का पूर्वानुमान
हालांकि, इस पश्चिमी विक्षोभ का प्रभाव सीमित रहेगा और प्रदेश के अधिकांश हिस्सों में मौसम सामान्य बना रहेगा. मौसम विज्ञान केंद्र के निदेशक शोभित कटियार ने बताया कि, "पिछले कुछ दिनों से प्रदेश में लगातार धूप खिल रही है और फिलहाल बारिश की कोई गतिविधि दर्ज नहीं की जा रही है. अगले चार दिनों तक भी इसी तरह धूप और शुष्क मौसम बने रहने की संभावना है. इन दिनों प्रदेश के अधिकतम तापमान सामान्य से करीब 2 से 3 डिग्री सेल्सियस अधिक चल रहे हैं. निचले मैदानी क्षेत्रों में अधिकतम तापमान 28 से 30 डिग्री, मध्य पहाड़ी क्षेत्रों में 20 से 24 डिग्री और ऊंचाई वाले क्षेत्रों में 15 से 18 डिग्री सेल्सियस के बीच दर्ज किया जा रहा है."
10 और 11 नवंबर को गिरेगा तापमान
मौसम विभाग के अनुसार, 9 नवंबर तक प्रदेश में दिन का तापमान सामान्य से कुछ अधिक बना रहेगा. इसके बाद पश्चिमी विक्षोभ के प्रभाव से विशेषकर मध्य और ऊंचाई वाले क्षेत्रों में तापमान में गिरावट आने की संभावना है. हालांकि, निचले मैदानी क्षेत्रों में मौसम में किसी बड़े बदलाव के आसार नहीं हैं.
शिमला में अगले 5 से 7 दिन बर्फबारी के आसार नहीं
राजधानी शिमला में बर्फबारी का इंतजार कर रहे पर्यटकों और स्थानीय लोगों को फिलहाल निराशा हाथ लग सकती है. मौसम विज्ञान केंद्र के निदेशक शोभित कटियार ने स्पष्ट किया है कि अगले पांच से सात दिनों तक शिमला शहर में किसी भी तरह की मौसम गतिविधि की संभावना नहीं है. ऐसे में फिलहाल शहर में बर्फबारी के आसार नहीं हैं. उन्होंने कहा कि जब भी शिमला या प्रदेश के किसी अन्य प्रमुख शहर में बर्फबारी की संभावना बनेगी, तो मौसम विभाग की ओर से चार से पांच दिन पहले ही इसकी जानकारी उपलब्ध करवा दी जाएगी.

It’s holiday season, not just on our roads, but also in the skies. And if sitting in bumper-to-bumper traffic is painful, sitting on a clogged toilet at 35,000 feet is a special kind of hell. Even if you’ve been spared the experience, you’ve almost certainly read horror stories about it, in media and social media. So, we have a suggestion for not just Tewolde Gebremariam, Air India’s new CEO, who this week made his first major public appearance, but all airline bosses. Speaking at Aviation India summit 2026, he underlined the airline’s big and long-term upgrade plans, to boost its international operations. But one thing that will lift the brand right away, is providing professional janitorial services for every long-haul flight.
It might sound odd at first, but hear us out. Right now cabin crews are assigned the responsibility to inspect toilets. IATA guidance suggests they should do regular checks, typically every 20-30 minutes. But cabin crew are already taking care of meal services, mediating seat-recline disputes, occasionally managing misbehaving passengers, on top of all their safety duties.
When airlines happily invest fortunes in lie-flat beds, mood lighting, and celebrity-chef menus, why leave the most basic human necessity to such a slapdash arrangement? Cabin crew, with many competing responsibilities, obviously cannot focus on maintaining the toilets well. And everything that they miss, translates into a very unpleasant flying experience for passengers, especially on a 6-16 hour flight. The only way to make sure this job is done properly, is to assign it to a specific person.
It’s true that in India, cleaning toilets isn’t a socially neutral occupation, but comes with a lot of caste and class baggage. In many parts of the world, though, it’s just another job. In many modern Indian offices too, not to mention airports, it’s a job with plenty of applicants. Why would it be any different when airlines advertise the job, especially if it comes with good training and salary? A dedicated sanitation steward – we suggest this as a job title that’s both to-the-point and respectful – wouldn’t just keep things spotless. They would also gently educate passengers on what not to flush, before things go south in the loo.
Last year, a Chicago-Delhi Air India flight was forced to turn around, after eight of its 12 toilets became “unserviceable”. Last month, a similar plumbing crisis forced a Madrid-Dallas American Airlines flight to divert to New York. And there are other such cases. What we are suggesting actually serves a global need. Sanitation management is not a priority for airlines, because it isn’t considered critical for airworthiness. But clean toilets are part of their most elemental duty of care, not some optional luxury. Do it before, as they say, sh*t hits the fan.

A climate chamber, virtual environments and technology that monitors the body and brain. Using these resources, researchers at Umeå University will identify ways to protect older adults' mental well-being during heatwaves at home in northern Sweden.
The project has received nearly SEK 9 million from Formas, the Swedish research council for sustainable development. It is led by Weizhuo Lu, professor and director of the Intelligent Human-Buildings Interaction Lab, IHBI.
In the IHBI, researchers use a climate chamber and virtual environments designed to look and feel like ordinary homes. This allows participants to feel as if they are at home, while researchers can carefully control the indoor climate.
How the body and brain respond
The lab is also equipped with physiological sensors and equipment for monitoring brain activity. Together with people's own accounts of how they feel, the technology helps researchers investigate the links between indoor heat, physiological responses, stress, fatigue and mental well-being.
"The strength of our lab is that we can study the indoor environment and human responses together. Our equipment allows us to investigate how people experience heat and which adaptations make a meaningful difference to their well-being," says Weizhuo Lu, who works at the Department of Applied Physics and Electronics.
The project brings together building research, psychology and neuroscience in the same experimental setting. By recreating and comparing indoor conditions, the researchers can gain a stronger basis for understanding the effects of heat and evaluating measures to reduce its impact.
Helping older people adapt at home
As many older people continue living in their own homes, adapting ordinary housing to a warmer climate is an important public health challenge. For older residents, heat can affect sleep, mood and the ability to cope with everyday life. The researchers will look in particular at differences in housing conditions, mobility, financial resources and social support, all of which influence people's ability to respond to heat.
A home should remain a place where people can rest, recover and manage everyday life, even during a heatwave. We want to provide advice that works in different homes and is realistic for people with different needs and resources."
Weizhuo Lu, professor and director of the Intelligent Human-Buildings Interaction Lab, IHBI
The project focuses on northern Sweden, where homes have traditionally been designed to retain warmth through cold winters, with good insulation and energy-efficient building envelopes. This can make them more difficult to keep cool in summer.
The results will support practical guidance on measures such as solar shading and ventilation, as well as on everyday ways of managing indoor heat. The advice will be developed in dialogue with older people, relatives, senior citizens' organisations and Umeå Municipality. It is intended both to help residents make informed choices and support municipalities and housing organisations in planning effective and accessible climate adaptation.

India's rising heat is putting unborn babies at risk of premature birth
Extreme heat during April 2024 was associated with around 10,050 additional preterm births in India. The findings deepen concerns about climate change's impact on maternal and newborn health.
The analysis by Zero Carbon Analytics, which examined the impact of the April 2024 heat event across India, Bangladesh and the Philippines, estimates that the extreme temperatures were associated with around 16,150 additional preterm births across the three countries compared with what would have been expected in a typical April.
India accounted for approximately 10,050 of these births.
More significantly, the researchers estimate that around 10,600 premature births across the three countries would not have occurred without the additional warming caused by human-induced climate change.
The findings offer another dimension to the growing health costs of global warming in South Asia, where extreme heat is becoming more frequent, prolonged and intense.
And researchers studying the toll of climate change on health underline that the consequences can extend well beyond delivery.
“Babies born prematurely are at greater risk of breathing difficulties, infections, developmental problems and long-term neurological complications. Preterm birth is also the leading cause of death among newborns globally and India,” said an epidemiologist with the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR).
India already carries a substantial burden.
Its preterm birth rate was estimated at 13% in 2020, among the highest in the world. The country accounted for around one-fifth of all premature births globally that year. Rising temperatures could add to an already significant maternal and newborn health challenge.
HEAT’S TOLL
The analysis estimates that India's April 2024 heat event was associated with a 3.6% increase in preterm births compared with a typical April. The impact was uneven across the country, with Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal and Jharkhand together accounting for around 65% of India's additional premature births.
West Bengal and Bihar experienced some of the sharper increases in the risk of premature delivery, while Uttar Pradesh's large contribution was also driven by its substantial population.
The researchers estimate that the average person in India experienced temperatures around 0.94 degrees Celsius above normal in April 2024. In some northeastern states, including Tripura and Mizoram, temperatures were approximately 2.7 degrees above the usual April average, translating into an estimated 11% increase in preterm birth risk.
The researchers also project that the problem could become considerably worse. By the middle of this century, climate change could contribute to around 15,300 additional premature births in India in a typical April, assuming no adaptation measures are taken.
A WIDER HEALTH CRISIS
The findings come against the backdrop of India's rapidly changing temperature profile. The country has been experiencing hotter summers, longer heat spells and warmer nights, with climate change making extreme heat events more likely.
The 2025 Lancet Countdown report on health and climate change found that, between 2016 and 2025, half of the heatwave days experienced in India were attributable to climate change. On average, people faced 10.6 heatwave days annually, of which 5.3 would not have occurred without human-induced warming.
The health consequences extend well beyond heatstroke and dehydration. Prolonged heat exposure increases cardiovascular and kidney stress, aggravates existing illnesses, disrupts sleep and reduces people's ability to work.
Changing temperatures and rainfall patterns also affect the spread of vector-borne infections such as dengue and malaria, while floods, droughts and declining food security can worsen malnutrition and disease vulnerability.
Pregnancy adds another layer of vulnerability.
“Heat can cause dehydration, increase cardiovascular strain and reduce blood flow to the placenta. Researchers believe these changes, along with inflammation and the activation of biological pathways associated with labour, may contribute to early delivery,” said the ICMR epidemiologist.
A synthesis of global studies cited in the Zero Carbon Analytics analysis found that every 1-degree Celsius increase in heat exposure was associated with 4% higher odds of preterm birth. During heatwaves, the odds rose by 26%.

When two heatwaves strike a young tree only a week apart, the damage looks very different from what appears when the same two events are separated by three weeks. That is the central finding of a new greenhouse experiment with two subtropical broadleaved species, Schima superba and Phoebe bournei, published in the journal Ecological Processes. Under the shortest inter-heatwave interval tested, net photosynthetic rate fell by 50.8 percent in S. superba and by 32.4 percent in P. bournei relative to unheated control seedlings. Photosynthetic rates were higher at longer intervals in both species.
The study was carried out at the Fujian Academy of Forestry Science in Fujian Province, China, using two-year-old seedlings grown in pots. Five treatment conditions were compared: an unheated control, a single three-day heatwave, and three recurrent-heatwave conditions in which two three-day heatwaves were separated by intervals of 7, 15, or 23 days. The first heatwave occurred on different dates among the recurrent treatments, but the second heatwave and the single-heatwave event were synchronized, and all physiological measurements were taken on a common final date, August 20, 2024. This design compared different treatment groups at one endpoint rather than tracking the recovery of the same seedlings over time.
A crucial structural limitation shapes every conclusion in the paper. Each treatment condition was implemented in only one semi-open greenhouse, and the six measured seedlings of each species within that greenhouse were biological subsamples, not independent treatment replicates. Treatment condition is therefore confounded with greenhouse identity, and greenhouse-to-greenhouse variation cannot be independently estimated. The authors state plainly that seedling-level comparisons describe variation among measured plants in these particular greenhouses and cannot provide valid replicated tests of heatwave-treatment effects. All treatment comparisons and exploratory statistics in the study must be read with this restriction in mind.
The heating itself was simulated with semi-open transparent greenhouses equipped with 3500-watt industrial heaters suspended about 1.5 meters above the ground at a 70-degree angle to reduce direct exposure of seedlings to heated airflow. During heated periods, daytime air temperature differences relative to the control were approximately 5 to 10 degrees Celsius, nighttime differences 0 to 5 degrees, with a mean reported air temperature difference of about 7.1 degrees Celsius. Soil water content in the heated greenhouses was roughly 6 percent lower on average than in the control greenhouse. The authors note that the treatments thus differed in both temperature and evaporative and soil-moisture conditions, and that these co-occurring differences should be considered when interpreting the physiological responses.
On the final sampling day, the researchers measured leaf gas exchange with a LI-6800 portable photosynthesis system, recording net photosynthetic rate, transpiration rate, stomatal conductance, and instantaneous water-use efficiency on mature, fully expanded sun-exposed leaves. Chlorophyll a fluorescence was measured with a Pocket-PEA fluorometer after 30 minutes of dark adaptation, yielding the maximum photochemical efficiency of photosystem II, Fv/Fm, the performance index PIABS, and a set of OJIP-derived energy fluxes per active reaction center and per excited cross section. Leaf samples were also collected to determine the activities of the antioxidant enzymes superoxide dismutase, peroxidase, and catalase, and the content of malondialdehyde, an indicator of membrane lipid peroxidation, using standard spectrophotometric assays on a fresh-weight basis.
The gas exchange results showed a clear interval pattern. In both species, net photosynthetic rate increased progressively from the 7-day treatment to the 23-day treatment, approaching the levels observed after a single heatwave. Under the 7-day interval, transpiration and stomatal conductance were approximately 32 and 36 percent lower than control in S. superba, and 37 and 46 percent lower in P. bournei. Transpiration rose with longer intervals in both species. Water-use efficiency, however, split the two species: it was higher at 23 than at 7 days in S. superba, shifting from negative to positive carry-over effect sizes, whereas P. bournei showed the opposite pattern, with a slightly positive effect size under the 7-day interval that turned negative at 15 and 23 days. The nominal species-by-interval interaction for water-use efficiency was significant at P < 0.001 in the exploratory analysis.
Oxidative responses also diverged between the species. Malondialdehyde content peaked under the 7-day interval in S. superba, indicating greater lipid peroxidation in that treatment group, but peaked under the 15-day interval in P. bournei, where its lowest level occurred under the 23-day interval. Catalase activity in S. superba was lower under the 7-day interval than after a single heatwave but increased under the 15-day interval, while peroxidase activity declined most markedly under the 15-day interval. In P. bournei, catalase remained relatively low under the 7-day interval and rose with longer intervals toward the control level, superoxide dismutase generally declined from the 7-day to the 23-day interval, and peroxidase stayed comparatively stable. Exploratory analyses found significant nominal interval associations for all four indicators, and significant species-by-interval interactions for catalase, peroxidase, and malondialdehyde, but not for superoxide dismutase.
Chlorophyll fluorescence told a partly different story. Fv/Fm reached its lowest value under the 7-day interval in both species; in S. superba it rose with longer intervals to a level comparable to the control under the 23-day interval, while in P. bournei it was higher under the 15-day interval than under the 7-day interval but decreased slightly under the 23-day interval. In S. superba, the energy flux parameters ABS/RC, DIo/RC, and TRo/RC were relatively high under the 7-day interval and decreased at longer intervals, whereas P. bournei maintained comparatively high values under both the 7-day and 23-day intervals with lower values under the 15-day interval. Notably, ETo/RC under the 7-day interval in S. superba was slightly higher than under the control and single-heatwave treatments rather than showing a reduction, showing that individual fluorescence parameters did not move uniformly. No significant species-by-interval interactions were detected for the fluorescence parameters.
The association analyses added a further layer of species contrast. In S. superba, catalase was the only antioxidant indicator significantly associated with photosynthetic rate, and the exploratory path model showed a negative catalase-photosynthesis association with a standardized path coefficient of -0.301, while Fv/Fm showed a positive association with a coefficient of 0.265. In P. bournei, peroxidase was strongly associated with photosynthetic rate, with a positive path coefficient of 0.287, and was also significantly associated with transpiration, stomatal conductance, and water-use efficiency. Stomatal conductance showed significant positive associations with photosynthetic rate in both species, with coefficients of 0.709 and 0.686 respectively. Random forest analysis identified stomatal conductance and photosynthetic rate as important predictors of peroxidase activity in S. superba, and Fv/Fm and photosynthetic rate as important predictors in P. bournei, while chlorophyll fluorescence parameters contributed 83 and 60 percent of the grouped predictor importance for malondialdehyde in the two species.
The authors are careful about what these patterns do and do not show. Because measurements were taken at a common endpoint, the observed differences represent interval-associated physiological responses rather than directly measured recovery trajectories. The exploratory exponential curves fitted to the interval-specific effect sizes had no residual degrees of freedom with only three intervals, so they are retained solely as visualizations, not as validated recovery kinetics. The modeled pathways are statistical associations rather than confirmed causal mechanisms, and the lack of independent greenhouse replication and repeated physiological measurements limits treatment-level inference and prevents direct characterization of recovery kinetics. The team calls for future experiments with independent replication, repeated measurements across broader interval ranges, and direct measurements of leaf temperature, reactive oxygen species, and photosystem repair. Within those limits, the study argues that evaluating heatwave carry-over effects in trees requires integrating carbon-water relations, oxidative stress, and photochemical performance together, because the response of any single trait can mislead.

Lagos and Ogun Residents Protest Critical Power Outages Amid Extreme Heat
Residents in Lagos and Ogun State protest prolonged blackouts worsening heatwaves. Citizens report hours without electricity, urging authorities to restore power before health risks escalate.
Residents across Lagos and Ogun states in Nigeria have launched widespread protests against prolonged power outages that have exacerbated extreme heat conditions. The unrest began in Somolu, Lagos State, on Thursday, as hundreds of citizens marched through streets chanting slogans against the deteriorating utility supply. This mobilization follows similar demonstrations on Tuesday in Lagos Island, signaling a growing public crisis regarding energy reliability during high-temperature periods.
Street Protests Demand Immediate Power Restoration
The core of the resistance emerged in Somolu, where residents displayed placards reading Give us light and Our businesses are dying while marching through affected neighborhoods. Viral video footage captured the intensity of the march, with participants declaring that they would not allow heat to kill them. The demonstration serves as a direct appeal for the immediate restoration of electricity, highlighting the urgency of the situation for businesses and households alike.

Individuals report severe drops in power availability compared to previous standards. Tolani Adewunmi, a factory worker in Berger, Ikeja, noted that Band A subscribers previously enjoyed over twenty hours of uninterrupted supply. She now receives only up to three hours, stating that the situation worsened immediately before heat announcements. Similarly, Ahmed in Somolu observed that steady nightly supply for ten hours has collapsed to less than forty minutes of continuous power.
Health Risks and Business Disruption Escalate
The prolonged lack of electricity has created dangerous living conditions for vulnerable groups. Ahmed warned that children and the elderly face serious health consequences due to unbearable nighttime temperatures. In Ewupe, Ogun State, Abdulsalam Balikis rated local supply as four out of ten, noting that restoration provides only four hours at best. Residents struggle to charge phones and access water, while the government has failed to implement effective solutions.
Two-Month Outages Cripple Daily Living Standards
In Ikorodu, a corps member named Olamiposi Yetunde reported that power interruptions have persisted for more than two months. She cannot store cooked food, charge devices, or iron work outfits, forcing her to borrow a neighbor generator and purchase expensive petrol. This dependency on costly fuel sources further strains household budgets, creating a cycle of financial and logistical hardship for affected families.
Household Adaptations to Energy Crisis
Residents have adopted drastic measures to cope with the energy deficit. Opeyemi in Ifako-Ijaiye stated she no longer stores food in freezers due to the lack of consistent power, cooking only daily quantities instead. Mrs Siyanbade in Isolo has been without electricity for over two weeks, relying on charging centers that pose risks of device damage or theft. She also purchases petrol to pump water, noting that the high cost leaves her with minimal funds for other necessities.

10 things to know about saunas, from stress relief to dehydration risks
A Cleveland Clinic family medicine doctor explains what sauna heat may do for stress, the heart, and pain, and when to skip a session.
Picture walking out of a grueling workout and into a small room filled with dry heat. Sweat beads on your skin within minutes. People have sought out rooms of this kind for centuries. A visitor may hope for more from the heat than damp skin. Anyone who climbs onto that hot bench has reason to ask what those minutes accomplish. A good sweat is easy to notice. Whether the heat does anything for the body or mind beyond that is harder to judge from inside a towel. The question matters most to the people who make the visit a regular habit, and to anyone weighing whether to start.
Warmth can harm as well as soothe, and the line between the two shifts from one sauna to the next. Each runs at its own temperature and uses a distinct style of heating. The surrounding environment adds a third variable. The three factors set the guidelines for a safe session, and anyone who ignores them invites overheating. A hopeful bather hears plenty about what a sauna might fix but has little way to tell which promises rest on research and which rest on hunches. Certain people also need a doctor's input before they sit down. A reliable guide has to separate what studies support from what they hint at, and it has to say who belongs in that group.
Cleveland Clinic, which describes itself as a nonprofit academic medical center, published a health explainer on saunas on Aug. 12, 2024, under its Health Essentials banner. Amy Zack, MD, a family medicine provider, supplies its medical commentary and outlines what time in the heat may offer and how to avoid trouble there. The article cites findings without naming papers, sample sizes, or numeric results, and it frames each benefit in hedged terms. Its scope covers eight possible benefits, the main types of saunas, the question of fat burning, the hazards involved, and three tips for users. The 10 items that follow draw on that material: the eight benefits, then the weight question and the precautions worth knowing before taking a seat.
Stress and anxiety
Illustration: Quartz
Anxiety may ease for sauna users, and family medicine provider Amy Zack, MD, points to evidence that saunas help people under heavy stress at work or in their personal lives. In her reading, the sauna experience appears to lessen anxiety. Her remarks cover pressure from the job and pressure from life outside it. She treats both as situations where time in the heat may make a difference.
Experts have not settled why a small, heated room would calm a stressed mind. Dr. Zack notes that several theories compete to explain the effect. One she raises centers on the soothing atmosphere of the sauna itself. Her account brings the setting into the picture alongside the temperature, which suggests the relief may come in part from the surroundings a person sits in.
Sleep may improve with sauna use, studies indicate. A better night's rest would stretch the benefit past the minutes a person spends on the bench and into the hours that follow.
Quiet reflection carries its own weight in Dr. Zack's telling. "Giving yourself that kind of introspective time is extremely successful in helping to mitigate anxiety, depression and burnout," she says. Her claim reaches past anxiety to two other strains, depression and burnout, that she credits such a break with reducing. Taken together, her remarks suggest a sauna's mental payoff may depend as much on the pause it creates as on the hot air around it.
Slide 1 body runs about 235 words, short of the 300-word minimum. The source supplies five points on stress (evidence for people in high-stress work or personal situations, apparent improvement in anxiety, competing theories including a soothing atmosphere, possible sleep gains, and Dr. Zack's quote on introspective time), and no approved web details cover this subject. Reaching 300 words would require padding or invented content.
Heart health
Illustration: Quartz
Sauna heat may strengthen the heart and help keep blood pressure within a healthy range, studies suggest. Both possible improvements flow from the body's response to temperature during a session. The person on the bench sets them in motion without lifting, running, or pedaling.
Dr. Zack traces the effect to a chain of physical reactions. Heat speeds the heart rate and sets off the sweating familiar to any sauna visitor. In her account, those reactions add up to a physiologic shift that resembles exercise. The same exposure, she explains, prompts the body to release anti-inflammatory agents.
Physical activity offers the clearest yardstick for what a sauna asks of the heart. UCLA Health reports that sitting in a sauna, along with the quicker heartbeat it brings, widens blood vessels and boosts circulation, much as a light or moderate workout does. The same outlet reports that findings gathered over several decades indicate sauna bathing produces a prompt, beneficial drop in blood pressure. On that view, a seated session and a gentle workout place comparable demands on the circulatory system.
Evidence for the heart claims remains incomplete, and Dr. Zack says so without hedging. She calls cardiovascular health an area that needs more research and leaves no doubt about that need. Her caveat follows her own account of how heat acts on the body. The placement marks the mechanism she describes as a working explanation awaiting confirmation.
Heart conditions change the picture for some would-be bathers. Dr. Zack advises skipping the sauna after a recent heart attack, and people with certain heart conditions belong on the list of those who should check with a provider before going in.
As things stand, a sauna session works as a possible complement to exercise for heart health, with too little proof to stand in for a workout.
Chronic pain and arthritis
Illustration: Quartz
Sauna sessions may relieve pain and stiffness for people who live with rheumatoid arthritis or ankylosing spondylitis, studies indicate. Ankylosing spondylitis is a form of arthritis that inflames the joints and ligaments of the spine. Its most common symptoms are pain and stiffness in the lower back, the hip, or both. Swelling and irritation in the spinal joints and surrounding tissue can leave the spine feeling rigid. Easing stiffness would target one of the two complaints most common among people with the condition.
Chronic pain outside those two diagnoses may respond to sauna heat as well. Dr. Zack points to some small studies that found such gains. She singles out dry and infrared saunas, which researchers believe push more blood into the muscles and calm muscle spasms. In her account, both types have shown results against chronic back pain. Her own description keeps the claim modest, and the benefit remains a possibility for any single patient.
Dry and infrared saunas deliver heat at different intensities. Traditional dry saunas burn wood or use electric heaters and run between 150 F and 195 F (65.55 C and 90.55 C). The majority keep humidity below 20%. Infrared models rely on lamps and settle at a cooler 110 F to 135 F (43.33 C to 57.22 C). Dr. Zack notes that infrared light leaves the surrounding air unheated and generates warmth inside the body. The gap between the two matters for anyone who struggles with intense heat. An infrared booth offers a cooler route to the same back-pain benefits she describes.
Ankylosing spondylitis has no cure. Its treatment options aim to control symptoms and may include exercise, physical or occupational therapy, and pain medication. A sauna's possible boost to muscle blood flow fits that symptom-focused approach and could give people with the condition another option to discuss with a provider.
Sore muscles
Illustration: Quartz
Sore muscles tend to respond to heat, says family medicine provider Amy Zack, MD. Her wording describes a frequent pattern without making a promise, and it leaves room for aches that outlast a session. The article counts calmer muscles among four possible payoffs that studies link to sauna use, a group that also includes lower stress, a sturdier heart, and pain relief.
Brain-derived neurotrophic factor, or BDNF, may explain the effect, according to the article. The body releases this substance when it encounters heat, and a sauna supplies warmth in abundance. The explainer does not describe how BDNF acts on tired tissue. The link remains a working idea, and readers should treat it as one.
Evidence for muscle relief looks slimmer than the support behind the pain-relief benefit. Dr. Zack offers her point as a general observation, and the article attaches no study findings to it. Sauna use for chronic pain, by contrast, draws on studies of people with specific joint conditions. A bather who expects looser muscles from the heat is acting on a reasonable hunch with a plausible chemical explanation behind it.
Soreness that surfaces after a delay following strenuous exercise carries its own name, delayed onset muscle soreness, or DOMS. The condition is a familiar companion for people who push their muscles hard during exercise. Its late arrival shapes what a post-workout sauna can do. A visit that follows training comes before that kind of ache has set in.
Heat and cold split the work of treating DOMS. Warmth boosts blood flow and loosens stiffness, and cold therapy targets pain and inflammation. A sauna sits on the warm side of that divide. Its likeliest contribution for a sore body lies in easing tightness. Bathers whose main complaint is swelling or inflammation would find cold therapy a closer match for that goal.
Brain health
Illustration: Quartz
Regular sauna use may lower the risk of neurocognitive diseases such as dementia and Alzheimer's disease, according to one study the article highlights. The finding concerns people who make the sauna a habit. It offers no verdict on the occasional session after a workout.
Dr. Zack cautions that this link needs more research before anyone treats it as settled. She attaches the same caution to claims about the heart, psoriasis, immunity, and weight loss.
She also raises a second, separate possibility. Sauna use may sharpen cognition, a matter of everyday thinking in the present. The study addresses the odds of developing a disease down the road. Each idea could hold up or fall apart on its own.
In her account, the physiological reasons behind any cognitive gain remain unknown. Her remarks on the heart and on muscle spasms name specific changes in the body. Her remarks on the brain name none. Without a known pathway, nobody can say how much sauna time a benefit would take, or whether it would last.
A lone piece of evidence and a missing mechanism limit how far the claim can stretch. They mark brain health as a field worth watching. Neither gives a reader a proven defense against dementia.
Lung function
Illustration: Quartz
Humid sauna air may help people clear mucus from their airways, according to family medicine provider Amy Zack, MD. She links the effect to moisture. In her account, a wet sauna may hydrate the respiratory tract, and a well-watered airway lets a person cough up phlegm with less effort.
Her phrasing leaves room for doubt about the mechanism. Dr. Zack calls the hydration effect "likely," a word that signals probability and stops short of proof. The benefit also hinges on the person in the heat. Moisture eases the work, and a cough does the clearing. The sauna aids a reflex the body owns. A working cough becomes part of the bargain for anyone hoping to breathe easier.
Damp air separates the setting Dr. Zack describes from the dry room most people picture. She treats a steam room as its own option, distinct from a sauna, and notes that it runs on humidity. She finds no clear sign that wet heat beats dry heat, or the reverse. Her breathing explanation singles out wet saunas and depends on water reaching the respiratory passages. Any easier coughing she describes belongs to humid heat, even though neither style wins in general.
Sensitivity to temperature swings may keep some people from gaining anything at all. Dr. Zack warns that anyone who struggles with changes in heat and cold may not tolerate a sauna. She urges every patient to consult a primary care physician or a specialist before trying one. Her advice covers all patients, with no carve-out for people who feel healthy. Someone hoping a steamy room will loosen a congested chest faces an extra step before the first session. The same vapor that may ease a cough can overwhelm a body unable to cope with shifting temperatures. A breathing benefit, then, begins in a doctor's office before it reaches the steam.
Psoriasis flare-ups
Illustration: Quartz
Psoriasis flare-ups may come under better control with sauna use, and one study suggests the heat can shrink the spread of plaques and patches across the skin. Dr. Zack tempers the finding. She says the topic needs more investigation and adds that little to no research exists, with support limited to anecdotes from clinical practice. Until that work arrives, the sauna counts as a possible aid for flare-ups and nothing firmer.
Flare-ups give psoriasis its rhythm. Symptoms can cycle between active stretches of several weeks or months and calmer spells when they fade or vanish. Plaque psoriasis tends to last a lifetime, and infections, stress, medications, or trauma can spark its worse periods. Keeping triggers such as stress and skin injuries in check may help limit symptoms. Patients learn to steer clear of other flare triggers, among them streptococcal infections, heavy drinking, smoking, and some drugs such as lithium and beta-blockers. A sudden halt to systemic corticosteroids belongs on the same list. Sauna heat would work on those swings and leave the underlying disease in place.
Standard treatment scales with severity. Creams or ointments can handle mild psoriasis. Moderate and severe cases may require oral or injected medicines or phototherapy. Doctors encourage people with plaque psoriasis to get moderate, safe sunlight, and brief supervised ultraviolet sessions may improve their lesions. Sunburn remains off-limits. Against that lineup, sauna heat brings a slim record of its own.
Sweat creates its own hazard for one form of the disease. Rubbing and sweating can aggravate inverse psoriasis, which appears as smooth, red patches in skin folds. A sauna session works by making the body sweat. Dr. Zack advises anyone with a medical condition of concern to get clearance from a healthcare provider before going in. People with inverse psoriasis could find a session's sweat working against the skin they hoped to settle.
Immune system claims
Illustration: Quartz
A stronger immune system appears on the list of eight possible sauna benefits, and the article says research shows saunas may help prevent the common cold and other viral infections. Dr. Zack keeps that promise at arm's length. She says more study must back up any claim that saunas improve immune function, and she attaches the same call for further research to her remarks on the heart, dementia risk, psoriasis, and weight loss. Of the five topics that draw her caution, immunity rests on the thinnest support.
The other entries bring more to stand on, whether a proposed mechanism, a study tied to a specific condition, or reports from clinical practice. Psoriasis can cite one study on flare-ups and anecdotal support from clinicians. The immune entry offers far less. It gives no explanation of how heat might help, no detail about the research behind the cold-prevention line, and no patient experience. Beyond that one sentence, its text amounts to a request for more evidence.
Immunity goes unmentioned in the article's subtitle, which names stress reduction, heart health, and pain relief as the draws of dry heat. The opening summary of what studies indicate covers stress, the heart, pain, and sore muscles, and it leaves immunity out of that rundown. The section's heading, by contrast, presents the improvement as fact. The text beneath it frames cold prevention as a possibility and holds the broader promise back until proof arrives. A reader skimming the headings could leave convinced of an advantage the body copy declines to confirm.
Sauna users who hope the heat will help them fend off illness have only limited research to go on, and Dr. Zack says more is needed before anyone can substantiate claims of better immune function. She urges anyone with questions about sauna use to talk with a healthcare provider, and a hoped-for immune boost makes a fair topic to raise. Her guidance calls for anyone with a medical condition of concern to get clearance before a session, whatever payoff that person seeks. Of the eight upsides on offer, immunity gives a bather the least reason to step into the heat.
Weight loss
Illustration: Quartz
Experts do not recommend a sauna as a weight loss tool, and Dr. Zack says no clear evidence shows that sauna heat burns fat. A couple of studies have looked at the question, she notes, yet none of them establishes that saunas help people slim down. She files the subject alongside several of the heat's other supposed perks as a topic awaiting more research.
The advice sets weight apart from stress relief, heart health, and pain, where studies point toward possible gains. On weight, experts advise against using the heat for that purpose at all.
Sweat drains water from the body during a visit, and a scale can register the drop. Someone who weighs in after a session may see a lower number for a short stretch. Dr. Zack calls the dip dehydration, a fluid deficit and nothing more. The number tracks water the heat has drawn off, and nothing in her account ties it to lost fat.
Proper rehydration erases the change. Dr. Zack says the lighter reading will not hold once a person replaces the fluids the heat pulled out. The pounds that seemed to vanish on the bench return with the water.
Timing creates the illusion. A scale reading from minutes after a session catches the body short on fluid, before drinking restores what sweat removed. A later reading, after the bather has drunk enough to replace the lost water, shows the gap closed. The two numbers measure hydration, and neither measures fat.
Chasing a lower number by staying longer in the heat would backfire. More minutes on the bench mean more sweat and a deeper fluid shortfall, with no clear proof of fat burned to show for it. Dehydration carries hazards of its own, and a bigger dip on the scale points to more of it.
A bather who reads a post-sauna drop as progress is reading a fluid debt the body must repay.
Dehydration and safety
Illustration: Quartz
Dehydration stands among the largest hazards of a sauna session, and it shows itself through thirst, headaches, muscle cramps, and confusion. Sweat drains fluid from the body for as long as someone sits in the heat. The defense starts before the door opens, with water ahead of a session and more once it ends. Electrolyte drinks offer another way to replace what the body sheds. The Forest Service cautions against sugary drinks and alcohol in hot conditions. Both can feed dehydration.
Short visits keep the strain in check. Dr. Zack suggests about 15 to 20 minutes and notes that recommendations vary. Newcomers can begin with five minutes and add time on each visit. Dr. Zack tells anyone who feels unwell, dizzy, weak, short of breath, or uncomfortable to leave the sauna and seek medical help. The Forest Service warns that extreme heat can overwhelm the body's natural cooling and lists heat cramps, heat exhaustion, and heat stroke among the resulting illnesses. The agency's signs of heat exhaustion include heavy sweating, weakness, pale skin that feels cold and clammy, a fast and weak pulse, nausea or vomiting, and fainting.
Sauna use carries little danger for most people, yet a few situations call for skipping it. Dr. Zack advises staying out after a recent heart attack or stroke, or after drinking alcohol. A broader group should talk with a healthcare provider first. The group includes adults older than 65, anyone under 16, anyone pregnant or trying to get pregnant, people with neurologic conditions such as epilepsy, those taking medication, and anyone concerned about male infertility. The Forest Service flags elderly people, the very young, and anyone with long-term health problems as more prone to heat illness. The age cutoffs on the sauna checklist mark both ends of that same range.
Heart conditions earn their own place on the provider list, covering heart disease, severe aortic stenosis, heart failure, and high or low blood pressure. The CDC urges clinicians to help patients with cardiovascular disease spot when heat may be aggravating their condition. The agency's examples include greater shortness of breath, unusual fatigue during exertion, and chest pain. The CDC asks clinicians to remind people with heart failure or kidney disease to watch for both fluid overload and dehydration in hot weather. Dr. Zack wants anyone with a worrying medical condition to secure clearance before a session.

CAVITE CITY, Cavite — The heat index in Cavite City is forecast to reach 39 degrees Celsius on Saturday and Sunday, 7 and 8 November, placing the area under the extreme caution category, according to the latest heat index monitoring report released by the Regional Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (RDRRMC) CALABARZON.

Los Baños, Laguna is also expected to experience a heat index of 39°C over the weekend, while Infanta, Quezon and Tanauan City, Batangas are forecast to reach 38°C.

India’s electric vehicle (EV) retail sales touched an all-time high of around 3.55 lakh units in October 2026, registering a year-on-year increase of 44.88 per cent, as EV penetration across the automobile market rose to approximately 11.5 per cent from around 6 per cent a year ago, according to data released by the Federation of Automobile Dealers Associations (FADA) on Friday.
October also marked the best-ever month for electric two-wheelers, three-wheelers, passenger vehicles and commercial vehicles, FADA said in its October vehicle retail report released on November 6.
The growth came amid strengthening buyer interest in electric mobility, supported by elevated petrol and diesel prices, improved driving ranges and EV prices increasingly approaching parity with comparable internal combustion engine (ICE) models.
FADA President Sai Giridhar said demand for EVs ran ahead of supply during the month, with vehicle availability emerging as the constraint rather than buyer demand.
Three-wheelers continued to lead EV adoption, with electric models accounting for 62.63 per cent of total three-wheeler retail sales in October, compared with 52.19 per cent in the same month last year.
Electric two-wheelers accounted for 9.65 per cent of two-wheeler retail sales, up from 4.66 per cent a year earlier. In passenger vehicles, EV penetration increased to 7.30 per cent from 3.55 per cent, while the share of electric commercial vehicles rose to 4.29 per cent from 1.67 per cent.
FADA said the broader shift towards cleaner mobility remained evident despite the year-on-year decline in overall vehicle retail sales in October. Total vehicle registrations stood at 31,72,466 units, down 23.80 per cent from October 2025 but 25.05 per cent higher than September 2026.
The association attributed the annual decline largely to a calendar effect, as October 2025 included both Navratri and Diwali, while Diwali falls in November this year.

The Spanish Meteorological Agency AEMET has issued an orange alert for rain on Sunday on La Palma, Tenerife, El Hierro, La Gomera and Gran Canaria, meaning several Canary Islands are affected. La Palma will be hit particularly early, as the orange alert there comes into effect as early as 9 pm on Saturday. The authorities are forecasting up to 30 millimetres in one hour and up to 100 millimetres within twelve hours. For all warnings over the weekend, they put the probability at between 40 and 70 per cent.
On La Palma, the warning level is rising day by day. Until 14.59 on Friday, a yellow alert is in place, with up to 15 millimetres of rain per hour, particularly in the south and west of the island. From 6.00 pm on Saturday, a rough seas warning will also be in place for the west coast, where winds from the south to south-west will blow at 50 to 61 kilometres per hour, corresponding to wind force 7. The winds will be strongest in the north-west, and the warning will remain in force until 3.59 am on Sunday. From 9.00 pm on Saturday, a yellow thunderstorm warning will be added to the orange rain alert.
An orange alert is in force on Tenerife, El Hierro and La Gomera on Sunday from 00:00 to 17:59. The Met Office forecasts up to 25 millimetres of rain in one hour in these areas, and – as on La Palma – up to 100 millimetres in twelve hours, with the rain mainly affecting the western and southern slopes, according to the authorities. During the same period, a yellow warning for thunderstorms is in force on these three islands and on La Palma. In the north of Tenerife, a second orange warning has been issued, this time for storm gusts.
Tenerife: Gusts of wind reach up to 90 kilometres per hour
In the north of Tenerife and across the whole of La Palma, an orange wind warning is in force on Sunday from midnight until midnight. The AEMET is forecasting south-westerly gusts of up to 90 kilometres per hour, with the strongest winds expected in the mountainous areas; on La Palma, these will also be felt in the north-west and along the east coast. A yellow warning, with gusts of up to 70 kilometres per hour, will be in place for both areas from 12 noon on Saturday.
Elsewhere on Tenerife, a yellow warning is in place all day on Sunday due to wind, specifically in the greater Santa Cruz area and La Laguna, as well as in the east, south and west of the island. The same warning level applies to El Hierro, La Gomera and the whole of Gran Canaria, with gusts of up to 70 kilometres per hour, particularly at medium altitudes and on the peaks.
Orange rain warning in Gran Canaria, yellow on the eastern islands
In Gran Canaria, the orange rain warning is in force on Sunday from 12 noon until midnight and covers the mountainous region as well as the east, south and west of the island. Up to 25 millimetres of rain per hour and up to 80 millimetres over twelve hours are possible, particularly on the western and southern slopes. In the north of Gran Canaria, as well as on Fuerteventura and Lanzarote, a yellow warning is in force during the same period, with up to 20 millimetres per hour expected; on Gran Canaria, the north-western slopes are particularly affected. All three islands are also under a yellow thunderstorm warning from 12 noon until midnight.
On Sunday, therefore, at least one warning will be in force across all the Canary Islands. In October, the AEMET issued an orange alert for El Hierro, La Gomera and the east of La Palma on a Thursday, at that time due to heavy showers and possible thunderstorms. Shortly afterwards, another orange-level rain warning was issued, accompanied by a severe Calima. This time, the orange warning extends across the whole of Tenerife as far as Gran Canaria.
When there is heavy rainfall in the mountainous regions of La Palma and Gran Canaria, the water in the barrancos quickly swells into raging torrents that can flow all the way to the coast. Particular caution is therefore advised in the ravines and along their edges.
